title: How to Grieve Well
excerpt: Grief is not a problem to be solved or a stage to be cleared. It is love with nowhere to go. The work is not to get over it. The work is to carry it.
body:
No one teaches us how to grieve, and then we are surprised that we do it badly. We expect ourselves to bounce. We watch a calendar and wonder why the third month is worse than the first. We apologize for crying at the grocery store. Somewhere we absorbed the idea that grief is a brief and tidy thing, a tunnel with a marked exit, and when it turns out to be a country we now live in, we assume something has gone wrong with us. Nothing has gone wrong with you. You loved someone, and they are gone, and grief is the shape that love takes when its object is taken away.

The Bible does not rush the grieving. David tears his clothes. Job sits in ashes for seven days before anyone speaks a word, and that silence is the only thing his friends get right. Jesus weeps at the tomb of a friend he is about to raise, which means even certain hope did not cancel his tears. Grief is not a failure of faith. It is faith feeling the full weight of a world that was not supposed to end like this.

## Let the loss be as big as it is

The first temptation is to shrink it. To say it could be worse, to find the silver lining early, to manage other people's discomfort by minimizing your own. Resist that. Name what you actually lost, not the polite version. Not just a person but a future. The conversations you will not have. The chair that is empty. The phone you still reach for. You cannot grieve what you will not name, and the size of your grief is simply the size of the love. Do not make it smaller to make others comfortable.

## Feel it in your body, on its own schedule

Grief is not only an emotion. It lives in the body, in fatigue and appetite and the strange heaviness in the chest. It comes in waves with no warning and no logic. A song, a smell, a date on the calendar, and you are undone in a parking lot. This is normal. The waves are not setbacks. They are the tide of a love that has not finished moving through you. Do not schedule your recovery. Let the body do what the body does, and be patient with it the way you would be patient with a friend.

## Refuse the false comforts

People will say things. Most of them mean well, and most of them will say something that lands like a slap. "They are in a better place." "God needed another angel." "At least they are not suffering." You do not have to accept any of it. You are allowed to receive the love behind a clumsy sentence and discard the sentence itself. And when it is your turn to comfort someone else, remember the ache of those words, and choose presence over explanation.

## Keep the relationship, do not sever it

Grieving well does not mean letting go. It means learning to carry. Talk to them. Keep a photograph out. Cook the recipe. Visit the grave or do not. Tell their stories until your children know them. Bonds do not have to be cut for grief to soften. The love does not end because the life did, and a faith that believes in resurrection has no business pretending the dead are simply deleted. They are not gone from God. They are not gone from you.

## Grieve in the presence of God, even when you are angry at him

The Psalms give us permission the church often does not. "How long, O Lord?" is a prayer. "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" is a prayer Jesus himself prayed from the cross. You can be furious with God and still be talking to him. In fact, talking to him angry is more faithful than walking away polite. Bring him the real thing. He can hold it.

**This week:** Set aside thirty minutes alone. Write a letter to the person you lost. Tell them what you did not get to say. Then read Psalm 13 out loud and notice that it begins with complaint and ends still trusting, and that both belong to the same prayer.

Grief does not have a finish line, and anyone who promises you one is selling something. What it has, slowly, is a changed weight. The loss does not get smaller. You grow stronger around it, and you learn to live with a hole that becomes, in time, less of a wound and more of a marker, a place where love once stood and still does. You will not get over it. You will carry it, and you will not carry it alone.

title: How to Sit With Someone Who Is Suffering
excerpt: The instinct is to fix, to explain, to make the pain smaller so we can stand it. Almost everything that helps requires us to do less and stay longer.
body:
When someone we love is suffering, our first move is usually for ourselves. We rush to say something, anything, because the silence is unbearable to us, and so we fill it with explanations and reassurances and verses we have not earned the right to quote yet. We tell ourselves we are helping. Mostly we are managing our own discomfort, and the suffering person can feel the difference. They can tell when you are present with them and when you are present with your need to feel useful.

Job's friends are the cautionary tale. For seven days they sat with him in the dust and said nothing, and that was the best thing they ever did. Then they opened their mouths, and everything went wrong. They explained his suffering. They built theology on top of his wounds. By the end God rebukes them, not Job. The lesson is hard and clear. Presence blessed him. Explanation harmed him.

## Show up before you know what to say

The most common reason people stay away from the suffering is that they do not know what to say. So learn this first: you do not need to know what to say. You need to come. Knock on the door. Send the text that does not require a reply. Sit in the hospital chair. Your presence says what no sentence can, that this person is not alone, that their pain has not made them untouchable. Waiting for the perfect words is just a respectable way of not showing up.

## Stop trying to fix it

Most suffering cannot be fixed, and the suffering person already knows this better than you do. When you reach for a solution, you are subtly telling them their pain is a problem you can solve, which means it is also a problem they should already have solved. Resist the fix. Resist the silver lining. Resist "have you tried." Your job is not to end their suffering. Your job is to refuse to let them go through it by themselves.

## Ask, then listen, then stay quiet

Ask what this is like for them. Then listen without preparing your response. When they finish, do not rush to fill the gap. Let the silence sit. Some of the most healing moments are wordless, two people in a room, one in pain and one unwilling to leave. If you must speak, reflect back what you heard rather than adding your own commentary. "That sounds unbearable" does more than a paragraph of advice.

## Do not borrow their grief and make it yours

There is a way of caring that turns the focus back on the helper, where you weep so hard the suffering person ends up comforting you. Feel it, yes. But carry your own reaction so they do not have to. The room belongs to their pain, not yours.

## Bring the practical, not just the spiritual

Love has hands. Drop off food without asking what they need, because they cannot answer. Mow the lawn. Take the kids for an afternoon. Sit with the patient so the caregiver can sleep. Suffering is exhausting in the most ordinary ways, and the casserole on the porch preaches a sermon the words cannot. Do not say "let me know if you need anything." They will not. Just do the next obvious thing.

## Stay past the funeral

Everyone comes the first week. The casseroles stop, the cards stop, and that is precisely when the loneliness arrives, when the rest of the world has moved on and the suffering has not. Mark your calendar for week six, month three, the first anniversary. Show up when no one else does. That is when your presence means the most, and it costs you the most, which is the point.

**This week:** Think of one person you have been avoiding because you did not know what to say. Stop avoiding. Send a short message that asks nothing of them: "I have been thinking about you. You do not need to reply. I am here." Then put a reminder in your phone to reach out again in three weeks.

We were not made to suffer alone, and the deepest thing we can offer one another is not an answer but a body in the next chair, unwilling to leave. You will say the wrong thing sometimes. Say it, and stay anyway. The staying is the love.

title: How to Pray When You Are Falling Apart
excerpt: When you most need to pray you can least manage it. The good news the church often forgets: prayer was never about having the words. It was about turning your face.
body:
There is a particular cruelty to the way prayer fails us when we need it most. In the seasons we could manage on our own, the words come easily. Then the diagnosis lands, the marriage breaks, the child is lost, and we kneel down and find nothing there. No words. No feeling. Sometimes no faith that anyone is listening. And on top of the suffering we now carry a second weight, the conviction that we are failing at the one thing that should help. Let me tell you what I have learned in those rooms, in others' and in my own. The collapse of your eloquence is not the collapse of your prayer.

## You do not need words

Paul writes that the Spirit intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words, precisely because we do not know what to pray. Read that again. Scripture anticipates the moment you are in, when language fails, and calls it not a failure but the ordinary condition of the suffering saint. A groan is a prayer. A sigh is a prayer. The single syllable "help" is a complete and sufficient prayer. God is not grading your grammar. He is receiving your turning.

## Pray the words you cannot find

This is why the Psalms exist. When your own well is dry, drink from someone else's. Open to Psalm 6, or 13, or 88, and read the words aloud even if you feel nothing. "I am weary with my moaning." "How long?" "Darkness is my closest friend." These are in the Bible. They are prayers God preserved for exactly this purpose, so that when you cannot compose, you can borrow. Pray them slowly. Pray them angry. Let David and the sons of Korah say it for you until you can say it yourself.

## Tell him the true thing, not the religious thing

Falling-apart prayer is honest prayer or it is nothing. Do not perform faith you do not feel. If you are angry at God, tell him you are angry at God. If you doubt he is there, say it to the One you doubt is there. The Psalms model raw complaint, accusation, even what sounds like despair, and God preserved every word. He would rather have your fury than your performance. The polished prayer that hides the real thing is the one that gets nowhere.

## Pray with your body when your mind is gone

When thoughts will not assemble, let the body pray. Kneel. Open your hands. Lie face down on the floor like Jesus in Gethsemane, who fell to the ground and prayed the same desperate sentence over and over. Walk and breathe a single line: "Lord, have mercy." The ancient church repeated short prayers for centuries because they knew the mind in crisis cannot hold long thoughts. Give it one true line and let it loop.

## Pray in the dark and expect nothing in return

Gethsemane did not feel good. Jesus sweat blood and asked for the cup to pass, and it did not pass, and an angel came not to remove the suffering but to strengthen him inside it. Sometimes prayer changes the circumstance. Often it changes only this: you are no longer carrying it alone. Do not measure your prayer by the feeling it produces. Measure it by the fact that you turned your face toward God instead of away. The disciples fell asleep that night and Jesus prayed on, alone, and even his abandonment did not stop the prayer. Yours will not be stopped either, by exhaustion or numbness or the long silence that follows. The reaching is the prayer, and the reaching counts.

**This week:** Each night before sleep, when you have no strength for anything else, read Psalm 13 aloud. It is six verses. It begins with "How long?" four times and ends, somehow, with "I will sing to the Lord." Do not force the ending. Just read both halves and let them be true at the same time.

Prayer in the collapse is not the prayer of the put-together person, and it was never meant to be. It is the cry of a drowning one, and the only thing a drowning person needs to do is reach. You do not have to swim. You do not have to find the words. You only have to turn, with whatever is left of you, toward the One who is already there.

title: How to Practice Lament
excerpt: Lament is the prayer the modern church forgot. It is not unbelief and it is not whining. It is the language faith speaks when the world is broken and God seems silent.
body:
A third of the Psalms are laments, and most of us have never been taught to pray one. We were given praise and thanksgiving and petition, the prayers for when things are mostly fine, and then when things were not fine we discovered we had no vocabulary at all. So we went silent, or we faked the praise, or we left. The church handed us a prayer language for half of life and acted surprised when we had nothing to say in the other half. Lament is the missing half. It is how the people of God have always prayed in the dark, and it is time we learned it again.

## Know what lament actually is

Lament is honest complaint addressed to God in the confidence that he is listening. That definition has three loads in it. It is honest, so it does not pretend. It is addressed to God, so it is not mere venting into the void. And it is built on confidence, so even at its most furious it is an act of faith, because you do not pour out your anguish to someone you believe is absent. Lament is not the opposite of trust. It is trust under the conditions of suffering.

## Follow the shape the Psalms give you

Most laments move through a pattern, and learning it gives you a path when you cannot find one. First, you turn to God by name. Second, you bring the complaint, the actual raw grievance, what is wrong and how much it hurts. Third, you ask, boldly, for what you want him to do. Fourth, most laments turn, somewhere, toward trust, not because the problem is solved but because the relationship holds. Psalm 13 does all of this in six verses. You do not have to manufacture the turn. Sometimes it comes. Sometimes, as in Psalm 88, it never does, and that prayer is in the Bible too.

## Say the complaint without softening it

This is the part we flinch from. We were trained to be polite with God, to wrap every grievance in a qualifier. Lament refuses the wrapping. "You have laid me in the depths of the pit." "Why do you hide your face?" "My tears have been my food day and night." These are not the prayers of weak faith. They are in Scripture, preserved by the Spirit, prayed by the most faithful people in the book. Stop protecting God from your honesty. He can hear the real thing, and the real thing is the only thing he can heal.

## Make it concrete, not abstract

Do not lament "the brokenness of the world" in general. Lament the specific thing. The empty side of the bed. The test results. The friend who betrayed you. The prayer you have prayed a thousand times that heaven has not answered. Lament is particular or it is performance. Name the actual wound, the actual person, the actual day it happened.

## Let it be communal, not only private

Lament was never meant to be only a solitary cry. Israel lamented together. The book of Lamentations is a city weeping over its own ruins. When you sit with someone in their suffering, you can lament with them, give voice to the grievance they are too exhausted to speak. And when you lead or gather others, make room for the prayer that does not resolve, so that the suffering among you do not have to fake a joy they do not feel just to belong.

**This week:** Write your own lament. Four short movements. Address God by name. Tell him exactly what is wrong, with no softening. Ask him for what you actually want. Then, only if it is true, write one line of trust, and if it is not true yet, leave it blank and let the blank be honest. Pray it three times this week.

The world is broken, and it is right to say so, out loud, to the One who made it and has not yet finished mending it. Lament is the prayer that refuses to lie about the wound and refuses to stop talking to God about it. It does not resolve the suffering. It does something harder and better. It keeps you in the conversation until the morning comes.

title: How to Wait on God
excerpt: Waiting is not the empty space between God's acts. In Scripture it is one of his primary works in a person, and the hardest one to receive.
body:
We hate waiting, and a culture built on instant everything has made us worse at it than any generation before us. We have one-day shipping and on-demand entertainment and the ability to summon a car with our thumb, and then God asks us to wait, sometimes for years, sometimes for what feels like forever, and we treat the waiting as a malfunction. It is not a malfunction. The Bible is, in large part, a book about waiting. Abraham waited twenty-five years for a son. Israel waited four hundred years in Egypt. The whole creation, Paul says, is groaning as it waits. Waiting is not the gap between God's work. Often it is the work.

## Name what kind of waiting this is

Not all waiting is the same, and it helps to know which one you are in. Sometimes you are waiting for a thing, the diagnosis, the job, the child, the restored relationship. Sometimes you are waiting for an answer to a question that may never come. And sometimes you are simply waiting for God himself, for a sense of his nearness that has gone quiet. The first kind tempts you toward control. The second toward despair. The third toward abandonment of faith altogether. Naming it honestly is the first step, because the false comforts that work for one are useless for the others.

## Refuse the two escape hatches

There are two ways out of waiting and both are traps. The first is to force it, to take Hagar instead of waiting for Sarah, to manufacture the outcome by your own scheming and call it faith. The second is to numb it, to check out, to deaden the longing so the waiting stops hurting. Scripture asks for a third thing, harder than both. Stay awake in the waiting. Keep wanting what you want. Keep asking. Do not force God's hand and do not stop reaching for it.

## Wait actively, not passively

Biblical waiting is not sitting still. The Hebrew word carries the sense of a taut rope, of tension and expectancy, like a watchman straining toward the horizon. "I wait for the Lord, more than watchmen wait for the morning," the psalmist says, and the watchman is doing something. He is keeping his eyes on the place where the light will appear. Waiting on God means keeping your eyes where his answer will come. Keep praying the prayer. Keep doing the faithful next thing. Keep your face turned toward the horizon.

## Let the waiting do its work in you

The waiting is not wasted, though it will feel wasted most days. Something happens in the person who waits that does not happen in the person who gets everything at once. Patience is not the only thing forged there. So is dependence, and the slow death of the illusion that you are in control, and a deeper hunger for God himself rather than merely his gifts. You will not see this while you are in it. You may see it only looking back. Trust that the field lying fallow is not the same as the field abandoned.

## Anchor yourself in a God who also waited

God is not impatient with you, and he is not unfamiliar with waiting. The cross was the long climax of a wait that lasted the whole length of human history. And between Friday and Sunday there was a Saturday, a full day when the tomb was sealed and nothing happened and the disciples had no idea that morning was coming. You may be living in Saturday. Saturday is real, and Saturday is hard, and Saturday is not the end of the story.

**This week:** Find the thing you are most tempted to force or to numb. Write it on a card. Underneath it write Psalm 27:14: "Wait for the Lord; be strong, and let your heart take courage; wait for the Lord." Put it where you will see it each morning, and each morning, before you reach for control, read it once.

Waiting is the discipline the whole modern world is conspiring to make us forget, and the people of God have always known it as a place of formation, not a problem to be eliminated. You may not get the answer when you want it. You may not get the answer you want at all. But the One you are waiting for is not far off and unconcerned. He is closer than your waiting, and he is not done.

title: How to Face a Hard Diagnosis
excerpt: The day the news comes, the floor drops out. You cannot control the disease. You can decide, slowly, how you will walk through what it asks of you.
body:
There is a before and an after, and the line between them is a sentence said in a quiet room by someone in a white coat. Before, you were a person with plans. After, you are a patient with a prognosis. The diagnosis does not just threaten your body. It rewrites your future, shrinks your horizon, and hands you a fear that wakes you at three in the morning. If you have just crossed that line, I am not going to tell you it will be fine, because I do not know that, and you would not believe me. I am going to tell you how people of faith have walked through this valley without pretending it is not a valley.

## Let yourself be afraid

The first thing the brave Christians around you may imply is that fear is a failure, that if you really trusted God you would not be afraid. That is a lie, and it adds shame to suffering. Jesus, in the garden, was "sorrowful and troubled" and asked for the cup to pass. Fear in the face of death is not weak faith. It is the honest response of a creature who loves being alive. Do not pile guilt on top of the diagnosis. Feel the fear, and bring it where Jesus brought his, to the Father, on your face, in the dark.

## Separate the facts from the catastrophe

In the first days the mind runs ahead to every worst case at once, dying a hundred deaths before any of them arrives. Bring it back. Get the actual facts: the diagnosis, the options, the questions you still need answered. Write them down, because you will not remember what the doctor said. Bring someone with you to appointments to be your second set of ears. Fear feeds on the unknown, and replacing the imagined catastrophe with the real facts, hard as they are, is itself a mercy. Fight the disease you have, not the ten you have invented.

## Take it one day at a time, literally

Jesus said not to be anxious about tomorrow, that today has enough trouble of its own, and a hard diagnosis is where that sentence stops being a platitude and becomes a survival strategy. You cannot live the whole illness today. You can only live today. Some days you can only live the next hour. Shorten the horizon to what you can actually carry. The manna in the wilderness came one day at a time and could not be stored, and that was not God being stingy. It was God teaching a frightened people to trust him for today and let tomorrow come when it comes.

## Let people in

The instinct is to protect everyone, to carry it alone, to not be a burden. Refuse that instinct. You were not built to bear this by yourself, and the people who love you would rather carry it with you than be kept outside the door. Tell your church. Let them bring meals and drive you to treatment and pray over you. Receiving help is not weakness. It is the body of Christ doing what it exists to do, and depriving them of the chance to love you is a kind of pride dressed as consideration.

## Hold your life and your hope at the same time

Faith does not ask you to stop fighting for your life. Treat the disease, take the medicine, do everything within reach. And underneath the fight, hold the deeper hope, the one that does not depend on the scan results. The Christian does not face death as someone with nothing on the far side of it. The empty tomb means the worst thing is not the last thing. You can fight to live with everything you have and still know that if the fight is lost, you are not.

**This week:** Write down the three questions that are frightening you most about your diagnosis. Bring them to your next appointment and ask them out loud, or call the nurse line if you cannot wait. Then read 2 Corinthians 4:16 through 18, where Paul names the wasting-away body and the unseen weight of glory in the same breath, and let both be true.

A hard diagnosis takes much from you, but it does not get to take everything, and the things it cannot reach are the ones that matter most. It cannot reach the love around you. It cannot reach the God who has already gone through death ahead of you and come out the other side. You did not choose this valley. You do get to choose, one day at a time, that you will not walk it alone or without hope.

title: How to Help a Friend Through Loss
excerpt: You will be tempted to find the right words and stay away until you do. The right words are not the point. Showing up, badly and repeatedly, is the point.
body:
When grief lands on someone you love, you want to help, and you do not know how, and the not-knowing keeps many good people frozen and distant at exactly the moment they are needed most. So they send a single card and then disappear, telling themselves they are giving space, when what the grieving person hears is that the world has moved on. Let me give you the practical love that actually helps, the kind I have watched carry people through the worst weeks of their lives.

## Go. Do not wait to be invited

The grieving rarely ask for help, partly because they are too overwhelmed to know what they need and partly because asking feels like a burden. So do not wait for the ask. Show up. Bring food. Sit on the porch. Come to the funeral and come to the house after, when the crowd has gone and the silence is loudest. Your presence is the message. You are saying, with your body, that this person is not alone and their grief has not made them an island.

## Say less than you want to

Your discomfort will push you to fill silence with explanation, and almost every explanation wounds. Do not tell them it was God's plan. Do not tell them they are in a better place. Do not tell them at least anything. The grieving do not need their loss interpreted. They need it witnessed. Try the short, true sentences: "I am so sorry." "I loved them too." "I do not have words." "I am here." And then, the hardest skill of all, be quiet, and let them talk, or let them say nothing.

## Help in concrete, specific ways

Never say "let me know if you need anything," because a grieving person cannot organize their needs into requests. Offer the specific thing. "I am bringing dinner Thursday, will I leave it on the porch or come in?" "I am taking the kids to the park Saturday morning." "I am coming to mow your lawn, you do not have to be home." Do the laundry. Answer the door. Field the casseroles. Make the phone calls they cannot make. Grief turns ordinary tasks into mountains, and the friend who quietly handles the mountains preaches louder than any sympathy card.

## Say their person's name

Many people avoid mentioning the one who died, afraid of reopening the wound. But the wound is already open, and the deeper fear of the grieving is that the world will forget. So say the name. Tell the story. "I keep thinking about the time she..." Let them talk about the person for as long as they want. You are not reminding them of a loss they had forgotten. You are honoring a love they are terrified will fade. The name is a gift.

## Stay for the long haul

Here is what almost everyone gets wrong. The support floods in for two weeks and then evaporates, and the grieving person is left alone right when the numbness wears off and the real pain begins. The casseroles stop. The calls stop. And month three is harder than week one. Be the friend who is still there at month three, at the first birthday, at the first Christmas, at the one-year mark. Put those dates in your calendar now. Send the text that says "thinking of you today, I know what day it is." That is the friendship that saves people.

## Tend yourself so you can stay

Walking with a grieving friend is heavy, and you cannot pour from a dry well. Feel the weight, pray, and find your own support so you are not secretly leaning on the very person you came to hold. Steady presence over a long season requires that you are tended too.

**This week:** Pick one grieving person, recent or not. Do one concrete thing without asking permission, drop off a meal, mow the lawn, send a specific memory of the one they lost. Then open your calendar and set a reminder for a date that will be hard for them, and decide now that you will reach out on that day.

Love in grief is not eloquent and it is not heroic. It is mostly just durable. It shows up, says little, does the dishes, says the name, and comes back next month when everyone else has gone. You will not fix their loss. You were never meant to. You were meant to make sure they never carry it alone, and that is a thing you can actually do.

title: How to Hold Onto Faith in the Dark
excerpt: Sometimes God goes silent and the lights go out and everything you believed feels like a story you told yourself. Here is how the saints have stayed when faith ran on fumes.
body:
There is a darkness the spiritual books rarely prepare you for. Not the darkness of unbelief, where you have decided there is no God, but the darkness of the believer, where you still believe and God has gone silent anyway. You pray and the ceiling is the ceiling. You open the Bible and the words lie flat. The worship songs that used to move you sound like noise. And you begin to wonder if any of it was ever real, or whether you simply outgrew a comforting illusion. If you are there, know this first: you are in good company. The saints have been here, and the Bible does not hide it.

## Know that the dark night is not the end of faith

The psalmist of Psalm 88 prays himself into total darkness and the prayer ends, with no resolution, on the word "darkness." That prayer is in your Bible. The God-haunted believers of every century have known a season the old writers called the dark night of the soul, when consolation withdraws and faith is asked to walk without feeling. This is not the failure of your faith. It is, strange as it sounds, often the deepening of it, the place where you learn to love God for himself and not for the warm feelings he used to provide. The dark is not proof he is gone. It is, frequently, where he does his deepest work unseen.

## Hold on by your fingernails, and let that be enough

When faith feels like it has nothing left, hold on with whatever you have, even if it is only the refusal to walk away. Faith in the dark is not strong feelings. It is mostly stubbornness, the decision to keep facing toward God when nothing in you wants to. Jacob wrestled all night and would not let go and said, "I will not let you go unless you bless me." That is the posture. Not certainty. Not warmth. Just a desperate grip that refuses to release. If all you can do is not let go, you are doing the work of faith.

## Borrow the faith of others

When you cannot believe, let the church believe for you. This is part of why we do not follow Jesus alone. Go to the gathering even when it is hollow. Let the songs be sung over you when you cannot sing them. Sit in the pew and let other people's faith hold you up the way the friends carried the paralyzed man to Jesus through the roof because he could not get there himself. There is no shame in being carried. The body of Christ is built for exactly this, for the strong to believe on behalf of the weak until the weak can stand again.

## Keep the practices when the feelings are gone

Do not wait to feel like praying before you pray. The feeling may not come for a long time. Keep the disciplines anyway, dry and dutiful as they are. Read the Psalm even when it is flat. Show up to worship. Keep the rhythms of prayer the way you keep eating when you have no appetite, because the body needs food whether or not it wants it. Faith is sustained in the dark not by inspiration but by fidelity, by the unglamorous decision to keep doing the next faithful thing.

## Wait for the morning you cannot see

The disciples on Saturday did not know Sunday was coming. They sat in the total dark of a sealed tomb and a dead Lord, and morning was already on its way and they could not see it. You may be living in that Saturday. The darkness is real and you are not imagining it, and it is also not the final word. "Weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning." That is not a promise that the night will be short. It is a promise that the night is not forever.

**This week:** On the nights faith feels gone, do not try to manufacture feeling. Instead, pray one borrowed sentence: "Lord, I believe; help my unbelief." It is the prayer of a desperate father in Mark 9, and Jesus honored it. Pray it as many times as you need to, and let it be enough.

Faith in the dark is the least glamorous and most heroic thing a believer ever does. No one applauds it. It produces no warm testimony, only a stubborn, unfelt clinging to a God who seems absent. But that clinging is not nothing. It is, perhaps, the truest faith of all, the kind that loves God not for the lights but in the dark, and waits for a morning it cannot yet see.

title: How to Care for a Dying Loved One
excerpt: Walking someone toward death is among the holiest and hardest things a person can do. It will cost you more than you have, and it is worth all of it.
body:
Few things ask more of us than caring for someone we love as they die. It is long, it is exhausting, it is full of impossible decisions and small indignities and a grief that begins before the death does. And it is holy ground. To accompany a person through the last door is to do something the world mostly hides and looks away from, and to do it well is one of the deepest acts of love there is. If you are in it now, or about to be, here is what I have learned from the bedsides.

## Be present more than productive

The temptation is to stay busy, to manage the medications and the appointments and the logistics, because busyness keeps the grief at bay. But what the dying need most is not your efficiency. It is your presence. Sit with them. Hold the hand. Be there when nothing needs to be done, when there is only the quiet and the breathing. Some of the most sacred hours of your life will be the ones where you accomplished nothing and simply stayed. Productivity is how we hide from death. Presence is how we honor the person dying.

## Let them talk about dying if they want to

Many people protect their dying loved ones from the subject of death, steering every conversation toward false cheer, and in doing so they leave the dying person alone with the one thing they most need to talk about. If they want to speak of dying, let them. Let them say their fears. Let them give instructions, make peace, say goodbye. Do not rush in with "don't talk like that, you're going to be fine." That sentence, meant as comfort, slams a door they were trying to open. Be brave enough to sit in the truth with them.

## Help them finish what needs finishing

The dying often have business to complete, and helping them complete it is a profound gift. The words that need saying, "I love you," "I forgive you," "forgive me," "thank you," "goodbye." The relationships that need mending. The faith questions that need a pastor. Make space for these. Bring the estranged child to the bedside. Call the minister. Help them say the things, because the unsaid things become the heaviest part of the grief that follows. Let them leave nothing essential unspoken.

## Tend the body with dignity

Dying is physical, and the care is often intimate and humbling, the feeding, the cleaning, the turning. Do it gently and without making them feel like a burden. The body that is failing carried this person through their whole life and still houses someone made in the image of God. Touch them with tenderness. Speak to them even when they cannot answer, because hearing is among the last senses to go. Dignity at the end is one of the last and best gifts you can give.

## Care for yourself, because this is a marathon

Caregiver collapse is real and common, and you cannot care for the dying from an empty tank. Accept help. Let others sit the shift so you can sleep. Eat. Step outside. Find someone to talk to about your own grief, which is real and which you are not permitted to suppress just because you are the strong one. Running yourself to ruin does not honor your loved one. Staying whole enough to keep loving them does.

## Entrust them to God at the threshold

There comes a point where the only thing left to do is to release them, to give permission to go, to commend them into the hands that made them. "Into your hands I commit my spirit," Jesus said from the cross, and you can pray those words over the one you love. The Christian does not hand a loved one into nothing. The resurrection means the door they are walking through opens onto something, onto Someone, and you let them go not into the dark but into the keeping of God.

**This week:** If you are caring for someone now, do one thing to make space for what is unspoken, ask them gently if there is anyone they want to see, anything they need to say, any fear they are carrying alone. And do one thing to sustain yourself, ask a specific person to take one shift this week so you can rest. Both are part of the same love.

To walk someone to the threshold of death is to spend yourself almost completely, and you will come out of it grieving and hollowed and changed. You will also have done one of the truest things a human being can do, loved someone all the way to the end and not looked away. That is not a small thing. In the economy of God, it may be one of the largest.

title: How to Handle Doubt
excerpt: Doubt is not the opposite of faith. Often it is the growing pains of a faith outgrowing the answers it was handed as a child. Here is how to hold it honestly.
body:
I came to faith from atheism, which means I know the inside of unbelief, and I know that the church often handles doubt in the worst possible way, by treating it as a sin to be repented of rather than a question to be honored. So the doubter learns to hide. He sits in the pew performing a certainty he does not feel, terrified that if he says the true thing out loud he will be corrected, pitied, or quietly written off. Let me say the freeing thing first. Doubt is not the enemy of faith. Handled honestly, it is often the road to a faith that can actually bear weight.

## Distinguish your doubts from your faith

The first mistake is to treat doubt as total, to feel one question and conclude the whole thing is collapsing. It is not. You can have a real doubt about a specific thing, the problem of suffering, a hard text, the silence of God, while the larger structure still stands. Name the actual doubt. Get specific. "I doubt that a good God would allow this" is a real, workable question. "I doubt everything" is usually just fear in a trench coat. Specific doubts can be examined. Vague dread cannot.

## Take your doubts to God, not just about him

You do not have to leave the room to doubt. The father in Mark cried out, "I believe; help my unbelief," and that contradiction, faith and doubt in the same breath, is one of the most honest prayers in the Bible, and Jesus answered it. Thomas doubted the resurrection out loud, refused to believe without evidence, and Jesus did not condemn him. He showed him his hands. Bring your doubts to God himself. Pray your questions. A God who can be questioned is a God strong enough to be trusted.

## Do the work of actually looking for answers

Some doubts persist simply because we never investigate them. We carry a half-formed objection for years and never read the people who have thought about it deeply. The Christian tradition is not afraid of hard questions, and it has been answering them for two thousand years. Read. Ask the pastor the real question. Find the thinkers, ancient and modern, who have wrestled with your exact objection. Faith is not a refusal to think. It has nothing to fear from honest inquiry, and much to gain.

## Sit with the doubts that do not resolve

Some questions will not be answered, and a mature faith makes peace with that. Job demanded an explanation for his suffering and never got one. God answered him not with reasons but with himself, with a presence so overwhelming that the questions, while never answered, were somehow no longer the point. There is a kind of trust that holds the unanswered question and keeps walking anyway, not because it has solved the mystery but because it has come to trust the One inside it.

## Do not let doubt make its decisions in the dark

Doubt loves isolation and the small hours. Do not let it deliberate alone. Tell a trusted believer, a pastor, a friend whose faith has scars on it. Stay in the community even when you feel like a fraud there. And whatever you do, do not make a permanent decision about faith in a temporary season of darkness or grief, when your judgment is least reliable. Doubt that is spoken aloud and walked through with others rarely ends where it started.

**This week:** Write down the one doubt that troubles you most, the real one, in a single honest sentence. Then do two things. Bring it to God in prayer, out loud, exactly as you wrote it. And bring it to one trusted person who will not flinch, and ask them to think about it with you. Do not carry it alone in the dark any longer.

Doubt that is hidden festers. Doubt that is honored, examined, prayed, and shared has a way of becoming the doorway to a deeper faith, the kind that has looked into the abyss and chosen God anyway, not out of naivety but with eyes open. The opposite of faith was never doubt. The opposite of faith is indifference, and the fact that you are still wrestling means you still care, and the fact that you still care means it is not over.

title: How to Keep Going Through Depression
excerpt: Depression lies, and it lies in your own voice. When the dark mind tells you to stop, here is how to keep putting one foot in front of the other, and where to get real help.
body:
Depression is not sadness, and the people who have not been there often confuse the two. Sadness is about something. Depression is a fog that descends with or without a reason, drains color from everything, and convinces you in your own internal voice that you are worthless, that nothing will improve, that the people you love would be better off without you. That last lie is the most dangerous, and I want to address it head-on before anything else. If you are having thoughts of ending your life, this is not a private spiritual failure to manage alone. In the United States you can call or text 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, any hour of any day, and reach a real person. Please do that. Then keep reading.

## Know that this is not a failure of faith

The church has too often told depressed people that if they prayed harder or believed more, the darkness would lift, which heaps shame on top of an already crushing weight. Reject that lie. Elijah, after his greatest victory, collapsed under a tree and asked God to let him die. The psalmist wrote, "Why are you cast down, O my soul?" Spurgeon, the great preacher, battled a depression he called a foe that walked at his side for life. Depression is not evidence that God has abandoned you or that your faith has failed. It is a real affliction, in the body and the brain, and treating it as a sin only adds cruelty to suffering.

## Get the help you would get for any other illness

If your chest hurt, you would see a doctor, and no one would call it weak faith. Depression is no different. See a doctor. Talk to a counselor. Consider medication without shame, because the brain is part of the body and sometimes the body needs treatment to do what it cannot do on its own. Faith and medicine are not enemies. God heals through doctors and therapists and yes, sometimes through a pill that lets the fog lift enough for you to pray again. Getting help is not a lack of trust. It is wisdom.

## Lower the bar to the next small thing

Depression makes the ordinary impossible, and then shames you for not doing it. Fight back by shrinking the task. Do not try to fix your whole life today. Get out of bed. Drink a glass of water. Open the curtains. Take a short walk outside, because the body and the mind are connected and movement and sunlight are not cures but they are real help. Each small thing you do is a quiet act of defiance against the lie that says nothing matters. String enough small defiances together and you are, against all the odds, still going.

## Do not believe everything you think

The cruelest feature of depression is that it speaks in your own voice, so its lies feel like your own conclusions. "You are a burden." "It will never get better." "No one would miss you." These are not insights. They are symptoms, the way a fever is a symptom, and you do not have to trust them just because they sound like you. Learn to say, "That is the depression talking, not the truth." You do not have to win the argument with the dark mind. You only have to refuse to act on its verdict.

## Let others carry you and stay in the light of community

Depression isolates, whispering that you should withdraw, that no one wants you around. Do the opposite of what it says. Tell one safe person the truth. Let them check on you. Show up to the gathering even when you feel nothing, and let the faith of others hold you when you cannot hold your own. You do not have to perform wellness. You just have to not disappear. Stay close to the people and the God who love you, especially when the dark mind tells you to hide.

**This week:** Tell one trusted person the real truth of how you are doing, out loud, no minimizing. If you have had any thought of ending your life, call or text 988 today, before anything else. And choose one small daily defiance, a walk, water, sunlight, getting dressed, and do it whether or not you feel like it. Feeling is not the entry fee.

Keeping going through depression is not glamorous and no one will see how hard it is. Most days the victory is simply that you are still here, still breathing, still putting one foot in front of the other while the fog tells you to stop. That is not weakness. That is one of the bravest things a human being can do, and you are doing it. The morning is not a feeling you have to summon. It is a fact you have to outlast, and you do not have to outlast it alone.

title: How to Find Hope When Nothing Changes
excerpt: Some suffering does not end. The prayer goes unanswered for years. Here is how to find a hope that does not depend on the circumstance finally turning.
body:
There is a particular exhaustion that belongs to suffering that does not end. The acute crisis at least has the dignity of drama; people rally, they bring meals, they pray fervently. But the chronic thing, the illness that does not heal, the marriage that does not mend, the prayer prayed for ten years into an apparently empty sky, that suffering wears a different kind of person down. The casseroles stopped long ago. The fervent prayers cooled. And you are left holding a hope that has been disappointed so many times you are afraid to pick it up again. How do you hope when nothing changes? This is the hardest question in this whole subject, and the church's easy answers are useless here.

## Stop pinning your hope on the circumstance

The first thing to understand is that the hope which depends on your situation finally improving is a hope that chronic suffering will eventually break. If your hope is "things will get better," and things do not get better, the hope dies, and you are left with nothing. The Christian hope is built on different ground. Paul wrote some of his most hopeful words from a prison cell he was never released from. His hope was not that the chains would fall off. It was anchored in something the chains could not touch. Move your hope off the circumstance and onto the One who outlasts it.

## Distinguish hope from optimism

Optimism is the belief that things will turn out well, and optimism is a liar in a world like this one. Christian hope is something tougher and stranger. It does not promise that the cancer will go into remission or the prodigal will come home, though sometimes, mercifully, they do. It promises that this is not the end of the story, that the God who raised Jesus from a sealed tomb is at work even where you cannot see it, that the suffering, while real, is not the final word over your life. Hope is not denial of the dark. It is a defiant trust that the dark does not get the last word.

## Grieve the thing that is not changing

Strangely, one of the doors back to hope runs through honest lament. Chronic suffering involves real losses that need to be named and mourned, the life you thought you would have, the version of yourself the suffering took. Let yourself grieve it. "How long, O Lord?" is not a failure of hope. It is the prayer of someone who still believes God is listening, who still expects him to act, who has not yet given up enough to stop asking. Lament and hope are not opposites. Lament is hope refusing to pretend.

## Shrink your horizon and look for the daily mercy

When the big rescue does not come, train your eyes on the small mercies that do. The strength to get through today. The friend who still calls. A moment of unexpected beauty. "His mercies are new every morning," Lamentations says, and notice that this comes from the most sorrowful book in the Bible, a man sitting in the ruins of his city. He is not hoping the ruins will rebuild themselves tomorrow. He is finding, in the rubble, that he is still being carried one more day, and that daily carrying becomes its own kind of hope.

## Anchor in the end of the story

The deepest Christian hope is finally about resurrection, about a day when every wound is healed and every tear is wiped away, and that hope is not escapism. It is the thing that lets a person endure unrelieved suffering without despair, because they know that even if nothing changes in this life, the story does not end in this life. The empty tomb is the guarantee that suffering is temporary and joy is eternal, that the verdict has already been rendered in your favor even while the appeal is still being heard.

**This week:** Each morning, before you let the weight of the unchanged thing settle on you, name one mercy from the day before, one small thing that carried you, however ordinary. Write it down. Build a list across the week. And once this week, read Lamentations 3:19 through 24, where a man in total ruin says "his mercies are new every morning" without any of his circumstances having improved, and let that be the model.

Hoping when nothing changes is the most stubborn form of faith there is. It is not the cheerful certainty that tomorrow will be better. It is the harder, deeper trust that whether or not tomorrow is better, you are held, you are not forgotten, and the story you are in does not end where your suffering does. The morning is coming. It may not be the morning you asked for. It will be a morning, and it will be enough, and the One who promised it has never once broken his word.
